lead: A thin-walled beam carries a transverse shear force S not at one point but spread along its walls as a shear flow q, in N/mm. The resultant of that flow acts along one line, and the point where that line crosses the section's axis of symmetry, or in general the point every such line passes through, is the shear centre. A load whose line misses the shear centre twists the beam as well as bending it. Wing spars, ribs, channel frames and control-surface hinges are all placed with this in mind.
prereq: You need: the bending stress σ = M y/I and the second moment of area of a thin-walled section, from the topic on bending of thin-walled beams.

sections.h3: Shear flow is force per length of wall

blocks.text: Take a short element of a wall of thickness t (mm) carrying shear stress τ (N/mm²). Because the wall is thin, τ is taken as uniform through t, and the force carried along each millimetre of wall is q = τ t. This is the shear flow. It is a force per length, so a wall of length L carrying a constant q transmits a force q L.

blocks.where: q is the shear flow (N/mm); τ is the shear stress in the wall (N/mm²); t is the wall thickness (mm).

blocks.text: Where does q come from? Look at a beam carrying shear S. The bending moment changes along the span at the rate dM/dz = S, so the direct stress σ = M y/I on one face of a slice dz long is not the same as on the other. A piece of wall cut off between a free edge and a point s along the wall is pushed one way more than the other, and only a shear flow on the cut can hold it. So q depends on how fast σ changes along the beam, not on σ itself: at the root of a cantilever σ is largest, but if the shear is zero there, so is q.

blocks.where: q(s) is the shear flow at distance s along the wall from a free edge (N/mm), positive in the direction of increasing s; S<sub>y</sub> is the shear force in the +y direction (N); I<sub>xx</sub> is the second moment of area about the centroidal x axis (mm⁴); y is the signed y coordinate of the wall element from that axis (mm); t is the wall thickness (mm). This form needs a section symmetric about x; the general form is in the chapter on open section beams.

blocks.text: Three facts follow. At a free edge there is nothing to carry shear, so q = 0. Along a horizontal flange y is constant, so q grows linearly. Along a vertical web y changes, so q is parabolic and peaks where the web crosses the neutral axis. At a corner the flow turns and carries on: q is continuous.

sections.h3: The resultant and the shear centre

blocks.text: Each element q ds is a small force along the wall. Add them all and the result is one force equal to the applied shear. Its line of action lies in the plane of the section. Two different shear directions give two such lines; the point where they cross is the shear centre, and every transverse load through it bends the beam without twisting it.

items: The shear centre is a property of the section shape, not of the load.
A doubly symmetric section (I-section, circular tube, rectangular box of uniform wall) has its shear centre at the centroid.
A singly symmetric section has its shear centre on the axis of symmetry, but not in general at the centroid.
A section made of walls that meet at one point, such as an angle or a tee, has its shear centre at that point: every q ds passes through it, so their moment about it is zero.
A load through any other point equals the same load through the shear centre plus a torque S × (offset), which twists the beam.

blocks.text: The shear centre is also called the flexural centre. For thin-walled beams it coincides with the centre of twist, the point about which the section rotates under pure torque.

sections.h3: The channel: why the shear centre sits outside the web

blocks.text: A channel has a web of depth h and two flanges of width b on one side. Under a downward shear, the top flange flow runs one way and the bottom flange flow the other way; each flange carries a force F = q<sub>j</sub> b/2, where q<sub>j</sub> is the flow at the flange–web corner. The two flange forces form a couple F h. The web carries the vertical shear. For the resultant to have no twisting effect, the vertical force must act at a distance e from the web such that S e = F h, on the side away from the flanges.

blocks.where: e is the distance of the shear centre from the web mid-line, on the side away from the flanges (mm); h is the web depth and b the flange width, both on mid-lines (mm); t is the uniform thickness (mm). The second form uses I<sub>xx</sub> = t h³/12 + t b h²/2, which neglects each flange's own second moment.

blocks.text: The centroid of the same channel lies on the flange side of the web, so the centroid and the shear centre lie on opposite sides of the web. A load through the centroid misses the shear centre by x̄ + e and twists the channel. A lipped channel adds short lips at the flange tips; their flows act against the flange couple and move the shear centre back towards the web. The method for any open wall is the same: start at each free edge with q = 0, build q along the wall, take moments of all the q ds about a convenient point, and equate that moment to S times the offset.

figure.caption: The worked example's channel under a 5 kN downward shear. Left: the flow runs along the top flange to the web, down the web and out along the bottom flange; the shear centre S lies 22.5 mm outside the web and the centroid G 15 mm inside it. Right: q grows linearly along each flange to 31.25 N/mm and peaks at 46.88 N/mm at mid-web.

examples.question: A channel has a web 120 mm deep and flanges 60 mm wide, all 3 mm thick (mid-line dimensions). It carries a vertical shear force S = 5 kN. Find (a) I<sub>xx</sub>, (b) the shear flow at the flange–web corner and at the middle of the web, (c) the shear centre position, and (d) the torque if the load acts through the centroid instead.
steps: Top flange, from its free tip (y = +60 mm): q grows linearly with s, q = (S/I<sub>xx</sub>) t y s in magnitude. At the corner (s = 60 mm): q<sub>j</sub> = 5000 × 3 × 60 × 60/1,728,000 = 31.25 N/mm.
Web, from the corner down to mid-depth: the area above the neutral axis adds t (h/2)²/2 = 3 × 60²/2 = 5400 mm³ of first moment. q<sub>mid</sub> = 31.25 + (5000/1,728,000) × 5400 = 46.88 N/mm.
Check the web total: the web carries ∫q ds = 2 × (31.25 × 60 + (2/3)(15.62) × 60) = 5,000 N = S. The flanges carry no vertical force.
Each flange force: F = q<sub>j</sub> b/2 = 31.25 × 60/2 = 937.5 N. Couple: F h = 937.5 × 120 = 112,500 N·mm.
Moments about the web mid-line: S e = F h, so e = 112,500/5000 = 22.5 mm. Formula check: 3b²/(h + 6b) = 10,800/480 = 22.5 mm.
Centroid: x̄ = (2 × 180 × 30)/(2 × 180 + 360) = 15.0 mm from the web, on the flange side.
A load through the centroid is 37.5 mm from the shear centre, so it adds a torque T = 5000 × 37.5 = 187,500 N·mm = 187.5 N·m.
examples.answer: I<sub>xx</sub> = 1,728,000 mm⁴; q = 31.25 N/mm at the corners and 46.88 N/mm at mid-web; the shear centre is 22.5 mm outside the web, on the side away from the flanges; a load at the centroid adds 187.5 N·m of torque.

traps: Taking the centroid as the shear centre. In the channel they are 37.5 mm apart, on opposite sides of the web.
Starting the integral at a corner. In an open section q = 0 only at a free edge.
Using the unsigned distance from the axis for y. y is a signed coordinate; below the neutral axis it is negative and the flow builds back down.
Placing the channel's shear centre on the flange side. It lies outside the web, on the side away from the flanges.

quiz.q: Define shear flow and give its usual unit.
quiz.a: Shear flow is the shear force per unit length of wall, q = τ t. Its usual unit is N/mm (the SI unit is N/m).

quiz.q: Why is the shear flow zero at a free edge of an open wall?
quiz.a: The edge has no neighbouring wall to deliver shear into it, and the complementary shear stress on the free face is zero, so τ and hence q = τ t vanish there.

quiz.q: Why does shear flow depend on the shear force and not on the bending stress at a section?
quiz.a: q balances the difference in direct stress between the two faces of a slice dz. That difference is (dM/dz) y dz/I = S y dz/I, so q is set by S. A section of large M but zero S carries no bending shear flow.

quiz.q: Use e = 3b²/(h + 6b) for a channel with b = 50 mm and h = 100 mm. Find e.
quiz.a: e = 3 × 50²/(100 + 300) = 7500/400 = 18.75 mm from the web mid-line, on the side away from the flanges.

quiz.q: A channel rib is loaded through its centroid. What happens, and name two fixes.
quiz.a: The load misses the shear centre by x̄ + e, so the rib twists as well as bends, adding torsional shear stress and stressing the attachments. In the worked channel the offset is 37.5 mm. Fixes: move the load line to the shear centre (a bracket outside the web), use a symmetric section such as an I or a closed box, or add a back-to-back channel.

beyond: Not for the exam. Hinge lines of ailerons and flaps are placed near the shear centre of the control surface so that air loads cause little twist. Search for "shear centre of lipped channel" and "centre of twist".
